TITLE: A KL-regularized Diffusion Model Fine-tuning Proposal using Importance Weighted Upper Confidence sub spectrum (IWUCS)
PROPOSAL:  We modify existing KL-regularized reward maximization methods for diffusion models to make the KL regularization tractable. By representing the diffusion process as a Markov chain, we approximate the marginal likelihood using importance weighted upper confidence sub-spectrum, which estimates the KL divergence as a sum of terms that corresponds to evaluating the KL divergence on the sub-trajectories of the diffusion process. This allows for backpropagating a tractable approximation of the KL regularizer, making it suitable for KL-regularized reward maximization.
CONTROLS: We compare our method, called IWUCS-Diff, with two baselines:
- A state-of-the-art policy gradient method for fine-tuning diffusion models (PGFT) with no KL regularization.
- Denoising flow in continuous RL (DFCRL), which directly optimizes the generative model for the desired distribution.
We also provide an ablation study of various components of our method and their effect on performance.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Given the KL regularization, we expect IWUCS-Diff to achieve better sample quality than DFCRL and state-of-the-art performance in terms of FID scores and Inception scores compared to PGFT, especially in challenging scenarios. We could fail if the KL regularization hinders exploration, causing the model to get stuck in a local optimum.

TITLE:  Integrating Denoising Flow and Importance Weighted Upper Confidence sub spectrum (IWUCS)
REVISED_PROPOSAL: We combine the advantages of the Denoising Flow (DF) and Importance Weighted Upper Confidence sub-spectrum (IWUCS), and explore whether this integration can lead to better fine-tuning performance for diffusion models.
- When steps of DF are added between IWUCS iterations, it allows for a more refined search of the diffusion space, and updates the IWUCS estimates, potentially making the policy more effective and reducing exploration-exploitation tradeoffs.
The revised algorithm interweaves IWUCS-Diff iterations (Kalman filter process incorporating KL regularization) with hand-designed transformation operators, specifically optimized with respect to certain metrics and constraints (adding energy constraints). This transformed flow achieves a non-degenerate upper-bound for the zero set, and lower-bounds for the variance, theoretically simplifying estimation in phase recovery and level set flows. Specifically, this refined approach assesses frequency parameter dependence.
CONTROLS: We evaluate our revised approach, IWUCS-DF, with the same baselines and ablation studies as in proposal 1, including the IWUCS-Diff method.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (approximately 2x due to increased complexity)
PREDICTION:  Integrating DF and IWUCS may significantly improve IWUCS-Diff performance in various aspects, especially sample quality and image/text synthesis task quality. However, we expect increased GPU-hours, making it infeasible for all experiments if very large datasets are required. It should be easy to combine it with a robust sampling technique, like split-DIFF.

TITLE:  Evaluating the Performance of Fine-Tuning Methods for Diffusion Models in Real-World Domains
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the performance of our proposed methods, including IWUCS, DF Robust, and Structure-aware fine-tuning, on a diverse set of real-world benchmarks in text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation. We assess their performance on metrics such as FID, Inception Scores, and Mean Squared Error (MSE) on real-world datasets such as ImageNet, IMDB, and ZINC.

CONTROLS: Compare baseline models with and without RMS normalization as well as different iteration counts and compute steps for various steer methods.

TITLE: Transformable Federated Learning for Heterogeneous Model Architectures
PROPOSAL: Implement a transformable federated learning framework that allows users to choose arbitrary model architectures while achieving collaborative knowledge transfer across tasks and models. The framework would utilize a novel adaptive mapping process to align model representations and facilitate information exchange among disparate models. This process would involve calculating the similarity between model embeddings using a faceted similarity metric (e.g., augmentation-invariant similarity) and adaptively transforming the representations to maximize alignment.
CONTROLS: Baselines would include non-IID data-only personalization methods (e.g., FedProx, SCAFFOLD) and existing model-agnostic federated multi-task learning methods (e.g., FedBert, FFM). Ablations would involve evaluating the effect of different similarity metrics and the adaptive transformation process.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The transformable federated learning framework would outperform existing methods in collaborative knowledge transfer across tasks, but might struggle with large architectural discrepancies where the adaptive mapping process becomes computationally expensive. Additionally, it may require significant hyperparameter tuning to optimize the alignment process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Compositional Contrastive Learning for Joint Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: Develop a compositional contrastive learning framework that allows for joint representation alignment among multiple models with heterogeneous architectures. This framework would utilize a hierarchical graph-structured model to capture the dependencies among multiple model representations. Compositional contrastive loss functions would be designed to encourage the alignment of representations at various levels of abstraction. Specifically, a graph neural network (GNN) would be employed to obtain a set of latent alignment vectors, which would be further refined using a InfoNCE-based contrastive loss function.
CONTROLS: Baselines would include existing pairwise alignment methods (e.g., InfoNCE, Gramian-based contrastive loss) and ablations would involve evaluating the effect of different graph structures and contrastive loss functions. Controls would also include evaluating the compositional framework on individual tasks to assess its personalization capabilities.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The compositional framework would significantly outperform existing pairwise alignment methods in joint representation alignment, showing improved generalization and robustness across tasks. However, it might be computationally expensive for large numbers of models and complex graphs, and could potentially suffer from overfitting if not carefully regularized.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Efficient Federated Multi-Task Learning with Adaptive Approximation
PROPOSAL: Revise the existing 'Transformable Federated Learning for Heterogeneous Model Architectures' proposal to incorporate an adaptive approximation mechanism. This would involve utilizing a meta-learning based approach to learn a set of precanned, task-agnostic approximation mappings, which would be dynamically selected and adapted to reduce the dimensionality of the representation space. The adaptive approximation mechanism would be trained jointly with the transformable federated learning framework to minimize knowledge loss and facilitate efficient representation alignment across tasks and models.
CONTROLS: The revised framework would be compared against the original transformable federated learning framework, as well as existing personalization methods (e.g., FedProx, SCAFFOLD) and knowledge distillation-based methods (e.g., FedDIL).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised framework would achieve improved efficiency and adaptability, significantly reducing the computational cost of representation alignment and facilitating more effective knowledge transfer across tasks and models. However, it might require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the trade-off between approximation accuracy and model expressiveness.

TITLE: Regularized Projection for Semi-Supervised Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel regularized projection mechanism for semi-supervised federated multi-task learning, enabling knowledge transfer and label augmentation across different tasks and models. A shared representation space would be learned via a regularized projection function that encourages both representation alignment and facilitates label regularization. This would be achieved using a combination of functional regularization terms (e.g., kernel-based regression, graph-based regularization) and pairwise constraints (e.g., label similarity, model agreement).
CONTROLS: Baselines would include existing semi-supervised federated multi-task learning methods (e.g., FedMix, FedSUE) and ablations would involve evaluating the effect of different regularization terms and pairwise constraints. Controls would also include evaluating the framework on downstream task learning and robustness to noisy labels.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The regularized projection mechanism would significantly improve label augmentation and knowledge transfer across tasks and models, leading to better generalization and robustness on downstream tasks. However, it might require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the trade-off between representation alignment and label regularization.

A decentralized collaborative filtering algorithm would be employed to iteratively update node importance scores based on global and local network information. The framework would adaptively assign tasks and knowledge transfer trust factors to each node based on its estimated importance, ensuring that knowledge transfer is robust, efficient, and balances topical relevance.

Controls would also include evaluating the asynchronous framework on real-world networks and dynamic edge cases.

However, its performance might be affected by the quality of decentralized node importance estimation and task adaptation mechanisms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Draft Model Cascade for Lossless Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of using EAGLE, Medusa, BiTA, and LayerSkip as self-derived draft models in a cascade architecture with retrieval-based statistical drafting at the bottom level. We will train each self-speculative technique on a set of task-specific training datasets (e.g. multi-turn conversation, machine translation) and then combine them into a multi-level cascade.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with standard speculative decoding and a retrieval-based statistical drafter alone, as well as a cascade of separately trained draft models.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant speedups over standard speculative decoding, especially with a well-configured cascade, but the speedups may vary across tasks and even within a single sequence, and might fall short of minimal retrieval-based drafting methods.

This experiment will serve as a starting point to determine whether existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods can be used to construct an effective cascade of draft models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling based on Auto-Generated Modeling
PROPOSAL: Investigate an adaptive scheduling approach that chooses the self-speculative acceleration technique, the draft length at each level, and the number of cascade rounds on the fly during inference. We will use meta-learning to train a separate model to predict these parameters based on the characteristics of the input sequence and the available acceleration techniques. The goal is to find the optimal scheduling configuration for each input instance.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with a fixed cascade schedule, as well as the top-performing fixed schedule discovered through a grid search.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive scheduling approach to lead to significant performance gains, especially when the input sequences exhibit diverse and task-specific characteristics. However, the performance may degrade when the meta-learning model fails to capture the underlying patterns in the data.

This proposal aims to address the second research question by improving the adaptability of the cascade speculative decoding approach while accounting for the variability in input sequences and acceleration techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Cascade Composition
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of combining different self-speculative acceleration techniques within the same cascade. We will experiment with various combinations of EAGLE, Medusa, BiTA, and LayerSkip, and assess how the properties of each technique (e.g. computational efficiency, accuracy) interact when used together. This will help us understand how to design effective cascades that balance competing objectives.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the standard speculative decoding, a single self-speculative technique, and the top-performing fixed cascade discovered through a grid search.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find composability benefits when combining techniques with complementary strengths (e.g. efficiency and accuracy) and challenges when combining ones with conflicting objectives (e.g. computational efficiency and accuracy).

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adaptive Draft Model Cascade for Lossless Speculative Decoding with Warmup
PROPOSAL: Introduce a gentle learning warmup phase into the adaptive draft model cascade to prevent catastrophic forgetting when the stronger draft models are added later in the cascade. During the warmup phase, the earlier draft models will adapt gradually to the stronger draft models' outputs, avoiding a sharp decrease in accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the original adaptive cascade scheduling, the cascade without warmup, and the retrieval-based statistical drafter alone.
COST: 0 extra GPU-hours, since this is an extension of the existing proposal
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive draft model cascade with warmup to perform at least as well as the original cascade and provide a noticeable reduction in the variance of the accuracy over training iterations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: On-Demand Model Selection for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Investigate a probabilistic model selection approach that dynamically chooses the draft model to use for each token during inference based on the changing characteristics of the input sequence. This approach will leverage the output probabilities of a separate prediction model to determine the suitable draft model for each token, enabling the adaptive selection of draft models based on the input's dynamics.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the top-performing fixed cascade discovered through a grid search, as well as the adaptive scheduling approach and the original adaptive draft model cascade.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect on-demand model selection to provide a noticeable speedup over the most adaptive existing approaches, especially in scenarios where the input sequence exhibits significant and unpredicted changes in properties.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Masking Strategies on Pretraining Time-Series Encoders
PROPOSAL: We will compare different masking strategies for pretraining time-series encoders, including random masking, structure-aware masking (based on temporal and channel dependencies), and masking based on importance scores derived from the data. We will evaluate these strategies using the SWaT (Sewater Treatment) dataset, which consists of physical Water and Wastewater sensor data for a water treatment plant. The goal is to assess how different masking strategies influence the quality of the representations learned by the encoder.
CONTROLS: Random masking, BERT-style random masking, and STASEE positional encoding baseline for comparison
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe significant differences in forecasting accuracy when using different masking strategies, with structure-aware masking outperforming random masking and BERT-style random masking. However, we also anticipate that the choice of masking strategy will not have a significant impact on the relative performance of different encoder architectures. If successful, this result would suggest that a well-designed masking strategy can improve the quality of the learned encoder representations, but that other factors such as architecture design and training objective have a more substantial impact on forecasting accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing Linear and Non-Linear Projection Layers for Time-Series Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of different projection layers for decoding time-series signals, including simple linear projections (LSTM, GRU), non-linear projection layers (GN, MHA), and attention-based decoders. We will evaluate these approaches using the datasets for weather forecasting (e.g., the Hybrid and Convective-Scale Ensembles (HyFS) dataset) and traffic flow forecasting (e.g., the Traffic Flow dataset), with the goal of determining whether non-linear projection layers can improve decoding accuracy.
CONTROLS: Simple linear projection layer (LSTM, GRU) and a vanilla MHA baseline
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that non-linear projection layers, such as attention-based decoders, can provide a modest improvement in decoding accuracy over simple linear projection layers, particularly when the forecasting task is difficult (e.g., short-term, no clear patterns). However, we also anticipate that the choice of non-linear projection layer can have a substantial impact on the overall performance of the forecasting model, and that different projection layers will specialize in different aspects of the forecasting task. This could lead to a new line of research focusing on jointly optimizing encoder and decoder architectures for time-series forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Channel-Dependent Architectures with Efficient Cross-Channel Attention
PROPOSAL: We will design a novel channel-dependent architecture that adaptively focuses on relevant channels for cross-channel attention, reducing the computational cost and improving forecasting accuracy. The architecture, referred to as CEChanAtten, will utilize a sparse attention mechanism to efficiently select informative channels. We will evaluate CEChanAtten on a variety of real-world datasets, including the solar power generation forecasting dataset (e.g., the FPl3 dataset) and the electricity transformer temperature forecasting dataset (e.g., the ETTF dataset), considering both short-term and long-term forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: Full-channel attention baseline (MHA) and a randomly selected subset of channels baseline
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect CEChanAtten to outperform both the full-channel attention baseline and the randomly selected subset of channels baseline, particularly when faced with a large number of channels. If successful, this result would demonstrate that efficient cross-channel attention mechanisms can effectively mitigate the computational costs associated with channel-dependent architectures, making them more viable for real-world time-series forecasting applications.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Channel-Dependent Architectures with Efficient Cross-Channel Attention
PROPOSAL: We will revise the proposed architecture CEChanAtten by incorporating a novel adaptation mechanism to dynamically adjust the channel weights based on the importance of the channels in the input data. This adaptive mechanism, coupled with the initial sparse attention selection, will enable the model to more effectively focus on informative channels and exclude irrelevant ones, leading to improved forecasting accuracy and reduced computational costs. We will evaluate the revised architecture on the same set of real-world datasets as before, including short-term and long-term forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: CEChanAtten without the adaptation mechanism ( baseline), CEChanAtten with the revised adaptation mechanism, and full-channel attention baseline
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised architecture to outperform the baseline CEChanAtten and the full-channel attention baseline, resulting in a more efficient and accurate cross-channel attention mechanism. However, we also anticipate that the adaptation mechanism may require careful tuning to achieve optimal performance, and the training dataset may need to be large enough to capture the distribution of channel importance.

TITLE: Joint Optimization of Time-Series Forecasting Architectures: Encoder, Decoder, and Training Objective Alignment
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel joint optimization framework for time-series forecasting models that considers both the encoder and decoder architectures as well as the training objective. The framework will incorporate a meta-learning approach to adapt the architecture to different forecasting tasks and datasets. We will evaluate the joint optimization framework on the same set of real-world datasets as before, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting, and electricity transformer temperature forecasting. Our goal is to determine whether a unified optimization framework can improve the overall performance of time-series forecasting models and simplify the model selection process.
CONTROLS: Separate optimization of encoder and decoder architectures (baseline) and the revised CEChanAtten architecture from proposal 3
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the joint optimization framework to improve the overall performance of time-series forecasting models by aligning the training objective with the architecture design, and to simplify the model selection process through the meta-learning approach. However, we also anticipate that the framework may require significant computational resources to optimize and that the performance may be task-specific.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating Focus Patterns with Physics-Informed Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop a physics-informed convolutional neural network (CNN) that takes into account the physical principles of focusing and sharpness by incorporating a focus pattern modeling module.
This module uses the known properties of image sharpness (e.g. contrast, frequency-domain behavior) in relation to depth and focus to inform the network's depth estimation. 
We will train this network on a large dataset of focal-stack images captured with a range of cameras, including industrial-grade cameras and high-end smartphone cameras, to cover a diverse set of real-world depth estimation conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare our physics-informed network to current state-of-the-art methods (e.g. DFNet, DFF-Net, STR rex), a physics-uninformed baseline that ignores focus patterns, and an ablation study where we disable the focus pattern modeling module.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (using 8 GPU nodes)
PREDICTION: Our physics-informed model should outperform physics-uninformed models in focal-stack depth estimation, especially in low-texture regions. However, the performance improvement might be minor in very simple scenes where texture-induced artifacts are not strong, and noise may dominate.

ACTION:  ADD 
TITLE: Probing the Impact of Defocus Maps on Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Design a new model that leverages defocus maps, learned through a self-supervised defocus simulation, to improve depth estimation in focal stacks.
This self-supervised approach will be paired with a distance-aware encoder-decoder architecture that takes into account the spatial layout and depth range of each pixel's neighborhood across the focal stack, and produces depth maps in an intermediate defocus-mapped space before refining them into sharp depth maps.
We will train and compare this model to current state-of-the-art methods on various real-world depth estimation benchmarks to quantify the contribution of defocus maps and distance-aware architectures.
CONTROLS: Compare our model to current state-of-the-art methods (e.g. DFNet, DFF-Net, STR rex), the existing model from proposal 1 with a pre-trained defocus simulation module replaced by a physics-informed module, and an ablation study to understand the contribution of self-supervised defocus simulation and distance-aware architecture.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (using 16 GPU nodes)
PREDICTION: Our model should show benefits over previous methods, particularly in scenes with complex focus patterns or multifocal effects, where defocus maps can suppress texture-induced errors. However, deep high-frequency awarded datasets might not be aided as deep focus based and classical depth have been poor there

ACTION:  ADD 
TITLE: Rethinking Gradient-Based Regularization for Focal-Stack Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Explore the effectiveness of adapting gradient-based regularization techniques, commonly used in depth estimation, to the spatial and focal dimensions of focal stacks. By accounting for the distinct patterns of focus cues in different depths, we aim to develop a more robust gradient-based prior that complements existing learning-based DFF methods.
To achieve this, we propose a novel spatial-focal coherence prior that penalizes inconsistency between neighboring pixels in different focal planes, while also promoting coherence within the focal dimension. Our prior is based on a combination of spectral and spatial coherence measures, derived from the focal stack's Fourier domain.
CONTROLS: Compare our novel spatial-focal coherence prior to existing gradient-based regularization techniques, evaluate its combination with model 1's physics-informed module, and study its interaction with the distance-aware encoder-decoder architecture from model 2.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (using 8 GPU nodes)
PREDICTION: Our spatial-focal coherence prior should effectively suppress noise and promote structural coherence in focal-stack depth maps, achieving state-of-the-art results in challenging scenes with complex focus patterns. However, evaluating its scalability to very large focal stacks or with very low quality input will require an adapted form.

ACTION:  ADD 
TITLE: Hierarchical Focus-Feature Fusion for Accurate Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Propose a hierarchical focus-feature fusion network that selectively integrates focus and spatial features from the focal stack to improve depth estimation accuracy. This network will consist of multiple focus-feature fusion modules, each exploiting different aspects of focus cues and suppressing texture-induced errors through a structured collaboration between spatial and focal attention mechanisms.
We will compare this hierarchical approach to current state-of-the-art methods on various real-world depth estimation benchmarks and study its performance in conjunction with models 1 and 3.
CONTROLS: Compare our hierarchical approach to model 2's distance-aware encoder-decoder architecture and model 3's spatial-focal coherence prior, evaluate its combination with model 1's physics-informed module, and study its interaction with existing gradient-based regularization techniques.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (using 16 GPU nodes with batch size 8)
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical focus-feature fusion network should achieve state-of-the-art results in focal-stack depth estimation by effectively exploiting focus cues and filtering out texture-induced errors, but struggling with noisy high-frequency contents; our model may have a minor overfitting on low Shot Environments that is strongly dealt with when word with noise

TITLE: Task-Agnostic Collaboration via Federated Ensembling
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we extend the knowledge-distillation-based approach that enables users to select arbitrary architectures by introducing an ensembling mechanism for the first time in the federated multi-task learning setting. We propose a server-side ensemble of task-specific predictors trained on shared representations obtained from a client-server federated distillation process. During training, the server utilizes a weighted-Liouville loss function that balances KL divergence with a term promoting similarity between soft labels and representation-based activation statistics, to encourage similar global representations across models. This encourages robustness to unseen tasks and architectures, and increases cross-task knowledge transfer. We predict that this ensembling-based framework will significantly improve model generalization and outperform existing methods for multi-task federated learning, particularly when dealing with a diverse set of tasks and user architectures.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to a state-of-the-art method for model-agnostic knowledge transfer and to the knowledge-distillation-based approach.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our ensembling-based framework should improve model generalization by around 10% on average, for both the few-shot and cold-start regimes, assuming users choose architectures that are not primarily frozen pre-trained weights with only partial fine-tuning for task-specific layers. If however users instead fine-tune primarily frozen pre-trained weights with minimal tuning of task-specific layers, we hypothesize this might reduce the gains to around 5% on average.

TITLE: Gramian-Based Contrastive Learning Extension for Multi-Modal Cases
PROPOSAL: We extend the prior Gramian-based contrastive loss approach to accommodate multiple models and modalities. We extend the traditional Gramian matrix to consider the dependencies among the representations obtained from all models and modalities, thereby allowing knowledge transfer across different tasks and modalities. We utilize a variant of the Fisher information matrix and leverage the properties of the Wishart distribution to define a novel Gramian-based loss function for multi-modal federated learning, enabling a theoretically grounded alignment of all representations produced by the users, regardless of their modalities and tasks. This approach explicitly models the representation dependencies among various models and modalities, mitigating the limitation of traditional pairwise alignment methods such as InfoNCE. We predict that this extended Gramian-based approach will achieve comparable or better performance than state-of-the-art multi-modal federated learning methods, while avoiding limitations such as requiring additional synchronization steps and initiator-based training.

PROPOSAL: We revise the modified Gramian-based approach to incorporate a hybrid strategy, combining both attribute-aware and knowledge-distillation-based methods for representation alignment. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Initial Experiment: Evaluating Existing Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding Methods
PROPOSAL: Evaluate existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods such as Lookahead decoding and SWIFT on a variety of real-world benchmarks (e.g., WikiText, Newsroom, BigPatent) across multiple Large Language Model (LLM) architectures (e.g., T5, RoBERTa, Switch Transformer) to establish a baseline for cascade performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard speculative decoding, lossless random sampling, and prompt lookup decoding.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (20 hours per experiment, 5 experiments in total)
PREDICTION: Lookahead decoding should show significant speedup over standard speculative decoding, while SWIFT may trade off some speed for improved output quality, with potential for up to 30% walltime reduction on suitable benchmarks.

Note: This experiment will help understand how well existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods can serve as base layers for a cascade, as well as their individual performance characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Unified Self-Speculative Decoding Framework
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that encompasses and integrates various self-speculative decoding techniques (e.g., Lookahead, SWIFT, LayerSkip, BiTA), allowing for flexible switching between them during inference and dynamic adjustment based on input characteristics (e.g., sequence length, task type). This framework should also support easy incorporation of new techniques and adaptive scheduling methods.
CONTROLS: Compare the unified framework against each individual method on a set of real-world benchmarks.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (25 hours for framework development, 10 hours per comparison experiment)
PREDICTION: The unified framework should significantly outperform individual methods on some tasks, particularly those that are well-suited to flexible framework components, and offer improved adaptability to unseen input types or sequences, potentially leading to average 10-20% walltime reduction.

Note: By providing a flexible and adaptable framework for combining different self-speculative decoding techniques, we can unlock the full potential of hybrid approaches and achieve more consistent performance across a wide range of tasks and inputs.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling and Draft Model Selection
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive scheduling and draft model selection mechanism that identifies the optimal combination of draft models and cascade configuration for a given sequence at inference time, based on factors such as task type, sequence length, and the availability of pre-trained models. This involves implementing novel heuristics or machine learning techniques (e.g., reinforcement learning, meta-learning) to learn optimal scheduling decisions.
CONTROLS: Compare adaptive scheduling against fixed cascade schedules and evaluate on a variety of tasks and sequence lengths.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (50 hours for adaptive scheduling development, 20 hours per comparison experiment)
PREDICTION: The adaptive scheduling approach should result in up to 30% median walltime reduction and improved performance on challenging tasks or long sequences, while also providing a more reliable and efficient foundation for lossless on-the-fly speculative decoding.

Note: By incorporating adaptability and learning into the scheduling process, we can dynamically adjust to the characteristics of the input sequence and task, leading to consistent and significant performance improvements across a wide range of scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revised Adaptive Cascade Scheduling and Draft Model Selection: Adding Transfer Learning and Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: Implement transfer learning to adapt the adaptive scheduling mechanism to new tasks and domains, allowing it to generalize beyond the tasks seen during training. Additionally, incorporate uncertainty estimation techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo dropout) to quantify the confidence of the scheduling decisions and adaptively adjust them based on the uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare revised adaptive scheduling against the previous version, fixed cascade schedules, and evaluate on a variety of tasks and sequence lengths.
COST: Additional 100 GPU-hours (25 hours for transfer learning and uncertainty estimation integration, 10 hours per comparison experiment)
PREDICTION: The revised adaptive scheduling approach should achieve even better generalization and reliability, reducing median walltime by up to 40% on unseen tasks and handling challenging cases more robustly.

Note: By adding transfer learning and uncertainty estimation, we can make the adaptive scheduling mechanism more robust and reliable, further improving its performance and making it more suitable for real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Cascade-Based Inference Acceleration on Edge Devices
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility and effectiveness of applying the unified self-speculative decoding framework and adaptive cascade scheduling to accelerate large language model inference on edge devices (e.g., smartphones, smart speakers), which are often limited by memory, computational resources, and power constraints. This involves adapting the framework to these new hardware platforms and evaluating its impact on task performance and user experience.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art inference optimization techniques and evaluated on a variety of edge device platforms.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (50 hours for edge device adaptation, 20 hours per comparison experiment)
PREDICTION: The adapted framework should lead to significant improvements in task performance and user experience on edge devices, such as up to 50% longer battery life or 20% faster task completion times, while maintaining high quality outputs.

Note: By pushing the boundaries of speculative decoding on edge devices, we can unlock new possibilities for real-time, on-device applications of large language models, further bridging the gap between the power of cloud-based AI and the simplicity of device-based interfaces.

TITLE: BERTScore-like metric for External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new metric, dubbed "Contextuality Score", analogous to the BERTScore metric, which measures the similarity between the generated text and the context tokens retrieved from the external knowledge base. Specifically, we will use the context tokens' embeddings and those of the generated output, compute the cosine similarity and average it over all tokens. This metric will be a dot-product based similarity score.
CONTROLS: For comparison, we will also evaluate the cosine similarity using only the retrieved context as input, and compare the results with the ones obtained using Devere (a strong retrieval-based hallucination detection method) as our baseline. We will also analyze the utility of contextual layers for diagnosing hallucinations by comparing scores calculated with contextual and non-contextual outputs from the retriever. 
COST: 2 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Contextuality Score is expected to reflect the external context utilization; we anticipate strong correlation between the score and hallucination occurrences, especially when compared to Devere baseline. Its limitation might be its tendency to get overwhelmed when confronting multiple, unrelated but linguistically similar context sources.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Cross-Model Validation using Hallucination Detection Datasets
PROPOSAL: Develop a new benchmark dataset by collecting and annotating a set of real-world examples of hallucinated responses from retrieval-augmented generation systems in the news summarization and data-to-text generation domains. We will design separate subsets or tasks on these datasets where each task will require the model to utilize a distinct portion of the external context. We will also collect high-quality human annotations to identify the hallucinated parts of the generated text and assign corresponding task-specific labels.
CONTROLS: As comparative baselines, we will evaluate existing hallucination detection methods (like Devere and ReDeEP) on the new dataset, assessing their performance by judging how accurately they detect overall hallucinations and identify the mis-INFORMED portions of the text, given the labels. This will help us see if any of these techniques apply to diverse domains, models, or tasks more strongly than others, contributing to identifying the relative strengths, and weaknesses of model domains.

TITLE:  Channel-Dependent Encoder with Causality-Augmented Cross-Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL:  This experiment aims to develop a new channel-dependent encoder architecture called Cacos-Net, which introduces a novel causality-augmented cross-attention mechanism to capture temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions more effectively. TITLE: Evaluating Baselines for Learning-based Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We will empirically evaluate and compare the performance of recent learning-based state-of-the-art DFF methods (e.g., Lu et al. (2020), Yao et al. (2020)) on a benchmark dataset like NYUv2 with real-world indoor scenes. The evaluated methods will include different types of networks (convolutional networks, flow-based networks, shape-from-focus approaches) that take a focal stack as input and output a depth map. We'll utilize quantitative metrics (mean absolute error, mean squared error, relative error, and depth accuracy in terms of a given threshold) and visual metrics (SSIM and PSNR) for evaluation, and consider the trade-offs between accuracy, smoothness, and robustness.
CONTROLS: We will use a set of heuristic baselines based on classic focus measures (e.g., sharpest focus in the stack, focus-score-based estimations) for ablation and comparison, including dense sampling baseline for the experiments, learning-based variants of the baseline models that employ gradient-based priors or spatial regularization for regularization and a dummy network that solely takes a single frame and predicts depth without any stack information.
COST: Estimated to require 1000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect the state-of-the-art learning-based DFF method to outperform the classical heuristics, but may still struggle with texture-induced artifacts, fine textures, and abrupt depth changes. If effective, we'll be able to understand the limits of these methods and what improvements are possible through using the underlying physics of focus in DFF.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Slice Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel attention-based module that incorporates focus relationships across multiple slices of the focal stack to disentangle texture-induced gradients from genuine depth edges. This Focal-Slice Attention Mechanism will selectively focus on the information from different slices to exploit the relationships between spatial and focal information. Specifically, it will learn the importance of each slice in the stack relative to the pairs of neighboring slices, forcing the network to selectively use the most relevant information. This mechanism aims to (i) suppress noise and irrelevant features, (ii) amplify the depth cues in the stack, and (iii) provide gradients that correspond to true depth discontinuities.
CONTROLS: We will use the set of learning-based baselines from proposal 1 with our Focal-Slice Attention Mechanism added on top. We'll also ablate individual components of the mechanism and use spatial-convolutional (and possibly full-resolution pre-trained weights) as an ablation to our proposed attention module, serving as one way to believe in the contributions of the Focal-Slice features.
COST: Estimated to require an additional 500 GPU-hours, bringing the total compute to 1500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our attention module should suppress noise, amplify relevant depth cues and considerably boost results over state-of-the-art DFF methods in terms of depth accuracy, but the evaluation generation may be successful on the real-world tasks and fail for as-yet unseen free-world only tasks and conceptual styles.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Focal-Physics Regularization
PROPOSAL: We revise the attention mechanism by incorporating a novel physics-regularization term, which aims to capture the underlying physical phenomenon that a scene point appears sharpest when the camera's focal plane aligns with its depth. This focal-physics regularization will be applied on both a global scale and a local scale to guide the network towards solutions that align with the physics of the focus mechanism. The global term will enforce the sharpness to be maximal when depth is optimal, whereas the local term will enforce the nadir point(s) in each local region to align with the maximal sharpness. This regularization term aims to (i) encourage the model to incorporate the physics of focus, (ii) reduce the model's reliance on weak texture cues, and (iii) provide an interpretable and principled depth-from-focus approach.
CONTROLS: We will use the set of learning-based baselines with our revised attention mechanism and physics-regularization term. We'll also ablate the physics-regularization term to understand its importance in terms of DFF outputs over those without. We will also compare our refined model to models from different “Learning-based DFFs” literature and numerous learned principled types like PSuRST-Packt instead.
COST: Estimated to require an additional 300 GPU-hours, bringing the total compute to 1800 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Our revised attention mechanism with physics regularization should yield more accurate depth estimations, particularly in regions with fine textures and abrupt depth changes, by aligning the model's predictions with the underlying physics of the focus mechanism.
